content: A chancre is a type of ulcer that develops without causing pain and is a hallmark of the primary stage of syphilis. This lesion typically appears about 21 days after an individual is first exposed to Treponema pallidum, the gram-negative spirochete bacterium responsible for syphilis. Chancres are highly infectious and facilitate the transmission of syphilis through direct physical contact with the lesion. These ulcers most commonly develop on or around the genitalia, such as the penis and vagina, as well as the anus and mouth. Without medical treatment, chancres generally resolve on their own within three to six weeks. However, their disappearance does not indicate that the infection has been eradicated, as syphilis can progress to more advanced stages if left untreated. In addition to their association with syphilis, chancres can also occur in the context of African trypanosomiasis, commonly known as sleeping sickness. In this case, the chancre forms at the site of a tsetse fly bite, which transmits the causative parasite.
